title: A Simple Microfluidic Chip for Long-Term Growth and Imaging of Caenorhabditis elegans
protocol: Design patterns 1 and 2 using rectangular shapes in a word processing software or CAD software.
Print photomasks with the help of a laser plotter on polyester-based film.
Cut silicon wafers into 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm pieces.
Clean wafers with 20% KOH for 1 minute.
Rinse cleaned wafers in deionized water.
Dry wafer pieces using 14 psi compressed nitrogen gas.
Dehydrate the pieces on a hot plate at 120 °C for 4 hours.
Cool two silicon pieces to room temperature before proceeding.
Place one silicon piece on the chuck of a spin coater and turn on vacuum.
Apply ~20 μL of hexamethyldisilane (HMDS) to the silicon piece.
Coat HMDS using the spin coater at 500 rpm for 5 seconds followed by 3,000 rpm for 30 seconds.

Place one wafer on a hot plate and coat it with ~1.5 mL of negative photoresist-1 using a spin coater at 500 rpm for 5 seconds followed by 2,000 rpm for 30 seconds to achieve uniform thickness of approximately 40 μm.
Hold the silicon wafers by their sides to avoid damage to the spin-coated layers.
Keep white lights turned off during wafer coating.
Spin coat silicon wafers with negative photoresist-2 using 1.5 ml at 500 rpm for 5 s followed by 2,000 rpm for 30 s to achieve a thickness of ~80 µm.
Bake the photoresist-coated silicon pieces on a hot plate at 65 °C for 1 min followed by 95 °C for 10 min.
Cool the baked pieces to room temperature before proceeding to the next step.
Store baked silicon pieces in the dark and do not expose them to white light.
Expose soft-baked silicon pieces to UV for 15 s using a 200 W lamp through photomask patterns 1 and 2 for flow and control layers, respectively.
Bake exposed silicon pieces at 65 °C for 1 min followed by 95 °C for 10 min with coated layer facing up.
Cool the baked pieces to room temperature before proceeding.
Soak silicon pieces in photoresist developer solution (1:3 dilution of developer in isopropanol) for 20 min.
Rinse the pieces with pure iso-propyl alcohol (IPA).
Gently blow dry using nitrogen gas (14 psi).
Expose silicon pieces to silane vapors by pouring 50 µL of trichloro (1H, 1H, 2H, 2H-perfluorooctyl) silane on a small plastic cup or glass slide.
Place the cup/slide inside a desiccator and incubate for 2 h.
Mix PDMS elastomer base with curing agent in a 10:1 ratio.
Stir the mixture constantly for 3 min to incorporate air bubbles.
Degas the PDMS mix in a desiccator for 30 min to remove all air bubbles.
Place the silicon wafers with the control layer in a Petri dish.
Gently pour a 5 mm thick PDMS mix layer on the silicon piece to avoid bubble formation.
Degas the PDMS mix in a desiccator to remove additional bubbles.
Place the silicon wafer with flow layer on the spinner chuck using 200-500 mTorr vacuum pressure.
Pour ~1 mL of PDMS on the silicon wafer for coating.
Coat the wafer using a spin coater at 500 rpm for 5 s, then increase to 1,000 rpm for 30 s to achieve an ~80 µm thick layer.
Bake both silicon wafers with PDMS layers in a hot air convection oven at 50 °C for 6 hours.
Wait for the pieces to cool down at room temperature after baking.
Cut the 5 mm thick PDMS layer from the silicon piece around the control layer using a sharp blade.
Peel off the PDMS layer from the silicon substrate.
Punch two holes of ~1 mm diameter in the PDMS block's reservoir using a Harris puncher to connect channels to gas lines.
Place the silicon piece with spin coated PDMS layer on pattern 1, with the PDMS-coated surface facing up, on a plastic tray.
Keep the punched PDMS block with pattern 2 (control layer) on the tray with molded side facing up.
Place the plastic tray inside a plasma cleaner.
Expose two PDMS surfaces to 18 W air plasma for 2 min under low vacuum (200-600 mTorr).
Apply vacuum until the chamber turns bright violet.
Take out the two plasma-treated blocks and gently bind the blocks by pressing the plasma-treated surfaces of patterns 1 and 2 together.
Bake the bonded patterns at 50 °C for 2 h in a hot air convection oven.
Cut the bonded device out of silicon wafer with pattern 1 and pattern 2.
Punch holes in the inlet and outlet reservoirs of the flow layer using the Harris puncher.
Place the plasma-exposed PDMS block on top of the cover glass.
Expose the blocks and the cover glass to 18 W air plasma for 2 min under low vacuum (200-600 mTorr).
Adjust vacuum pressure to see a violet chamber.
Clean the cover glass with IPA and blow dry using nitrogen gas at 14 psi.
Place the plasma-exposed PDMS block on top of the cleaned cover glass.
Bake the bonded structure in an oven at 50 °C for 2 h.
Store the device in a clean chamber for any future experiment.
Put the device on a stereomicroscope.
Attach tubings to the device as described.
Connect a micro flex tube to a compressed nitrogen gas line at one end.
Connect a three-way connector to the other end of the micro flex tube.
Connect tubes 1 and 2 of the three-way connectors to the trap and isolating membranes, respectively.
Connect two micro flex tubes to the two outlet ports of the three-way stopcock.
Connect the other ends of these tubes to an 8 mm long 18 G needle.
Fill the flow layer with M9 buffer using a micropipette through the inlet port.
Fill both tubes with DI water through the end connected to the needles.
Insert the two needles into the punched holes, connecting the isolating and trapping membrane, respectively.
Open the nitrogen gas regulator at 14 psi and turn the three-way valve from tube 1 to push the water into the device through the microfluidic channels in the control layers.
Wait until water fills the channel without any air droplets present.
Once channels are completely filled with water, consider them primed.
Release pressure using the three-way stopcock once channels are filled and primed.
Remove bubbles from the flow layer by flowing additional media through the flow channel.
Grow C. elegans on nematode growth medium (NGM) Petri plates with E. coli OP50 as the food source at 22 °C.
Transfer a few hermaphrodites or chunk a small amount of agar with a few animals to a new NGM plate with an OP50 lawn.
Check the NGM plate for animal growth and C. elegans eggs after 3-5 days.
Collect approximately 30 eggs from a plate and transfer them to a fresh NGM plate with OP50 lawn.
Transfer all unhatched eggs from the plate every 2 hours to a new plate for synchronization.
Pick animals between 14-16 h and 28-30 h after hatching for larval 2 (L2) and larval 3 (L3) stages, respectively.
Mount a growth and imaging microfluidic device on an inverted microscope.
View pattern 2 at low magnifications (4x or 10x).
Ensure that the channels are filled with clean distilled water.
Prepare a fresh 1 L solution of S medium using specified quantities of potassium citrate, trace metals solution, CaCl2, and MgSO4 under sterile conditions.
Do not autoclave the S medium.
Fill the flow channel with growth media (S medium) 10 min before the experiment.
Avoid any air bubbles in the flow channel.
Flow additional medium if needed to remove air bubbles.
Pick a single animal from the required developmental stage using a micropipette and transfer it into the flow channel through the inlet hole.
Monitor the animal position in the flow channel using a low magnification objective.
Flow additional medium through the inlet or outlet to push the animal and position it within the flow channel restricted between the two isolation membranes.
Open the three-way stopcock to apply 14 psi pressure in the isolation channels.
Push the membranes down into the flow channel.
Use a single colony of E. coli OP50 from a streaked plate to inoculate 250 mL of L Broth.
Grow the inoculated culture overnight at 37 °C.
Aliquot 500 µL of OP50 culture into 1.5 mL sterile centrifuge tubes.
Store the aliquot for 2 weeks at 4 °C.
Centrifuge OP50 culture at 1.3 x g for 5 min to pellet down the bacteria.
Dissolve the pellet with 1 mL of fresh S medium (0.5x dilution).
Store the diluted OP50 at room temperature for 3-4 days.
Use this diluted OP50 to feed C. elegans inside microfluidic devices.
Leave a drop of S medium on top of the inlet and outlet reservoirs to reduce evaporation.
Take diluted OP50 solution in a 10 µL micropipette.
Remove the micro tip filled with the OP50 solution from the pipette.
Press-fit the tip into the inlet reservoir.
Insert another micropipette tip with 10 µL of food solution into the outlet reservoir.
Seal the tip head applying pressure using a finger to ensure continuity of food solutions without any air gap.
Change the micropipette tip with OP50 solution every day that is not older than 3-4 days.
Fill an additional 20-30 µL of food solution in both the tips.
Add or remove food solution to and from the micropipette tip to adjust the gradient.
Monitor the flow of bacteria through the partially closed isolation membranes using bright-field images.
Replace micropipette tips at the inlet and outlet with new ones filled with freshly prepared food supplies if no bacteria or flow is present in the channel.
Locate a single C. elegans animal in the growth channel at low magnifications.
Adjust food solution heights in the two micropipette tips connected to the inlet and outlet reservoirs.
Push the animal in the required direction using hydrostatic pressure differences in the flow channel.
Position the animal at the center of the trapping membrane and monitor its swimming behavior using a 4x objective.
Turn the three-way stopcock to increase the pressure in the trap channel slowly.
Immobilize the animal under the trap membrane in a straight posture along the growth channel boundary wall.
Carry the device on a microscope stage.
Set up an inverted microscope with the necessary optical components for imaging.
Acquire time-lapse fluorescence images to capture cellular and sub-cellular events.
Use a 60x, 1.4 numerical aperture (NA) objective for imaging C. elegans neurons.
Employ a 488 nm wavelength laser with 7%-10% power during imaging.
Capture images at a speed of 4 frames per second using the microscope software.
Release the trapping pressure and monitor animal locomotion under low magnifications.
Maintain the animal within the region defined by isolating membranes at 14 psi.
Adjust the volume of food solution in micropipette tips for slow gravity-driven flow.
Ensure a height difference between food solutions in inlet and outlet micropipettes (typically 1-5 mm).
Visualize the flow under bright-field from the bacteria's flow pattern in the growth channel.
Release isolation and trapping pressure after predetermined time intervals.
Flush the channel with M9 buffer to remove bacteria.
Push the animal through the inlet reservoir using M9 buffer.
Recover the animal from the reservoir and place it on a fresh NGM plate for further health monitoring.
Flush the channel multiple times with M9 buffer to ensure cleanliness.
Rinse the flow channel with 70% ethyl alcohol diluted in distilled water.
Dry the channels by pushing air through them using a syringe.
Store the device in a dry, dust-free place for future use.
Use FIJI ImageJ software for tiff image analysis.
Open tiff images of PVD time-lapse images from wdIs51 animals in Fiji ImageJ.
Select Image tab > Stacks > Z project to extract the best planes from the stack of z-planes showing primary processes.
Screen the entire series of images and find specific image frames that successfully cover the entire neuronal processes using overlapping sections of the animal image frames.
Select Plugin > Analyze > Cell Counter from the FIJI toolbar.
Select Initialize > Counters > Type1, then mark the secondary branches.
Select Type 2 and mark Quaternary.
Click Results window showing counts of all branches (Supplementary Figure 2).
Open the next overlapping image and count the remaining branches.
Identify and count the total number of primary branches present in the early larval stages of C. elegans.
Perform similar analysis for images of secondary and quaternary processes in older animals.
Calculate the distance between PVD cell bodies in wdIs51 animals.
Draw a segmented line from the PVD cell body to PVC CB using ImageJ.
Select overlapping images to cover the entire animal length from head-to-tail.
Measure the lengths of all segmented lines along neuronal processes.
Add the lengths of all segments to calculate the total distance between PVD and PVC CBs for each time point.
Load images in Fiji for neuron length measurement of TRNs in jsIs609 animals.
Draw a segmented line along PLMs from cell body to the centroid of the first mitochondrion.
Calculate the length of the line for the first distance value.
Draw a segmented line from the center of one mitochondrion to the next until the end of the neuronal process.
Add all lengths to calculate the total neuronal process length.
Load all vulval images in Fiji for cell lineage analysis.
Extract the best focus image of cells from time-lapse images of multiple z-planes.
Represent the data as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM).
Calculate statistical significance using one-way ANOVA for more than two samples.
Calculate statistical significance using a two-sample t-test for a pair of samples.
Denote significance by p-value < 0.05 (*).
Denote significance by p-value < 0.005 (**).
Denote significance by p-value > 0.05 (ns, not significant).
